siblings.title: The staged ladder: what each rung of a Windows→Linux move actually proves
siblings.summary: A rung-by-rung ladder from WSL2 to full switch, with what each rung proves, what it structurally hides, the go/no-go signal, and the cost of retreating.

siblings.title: WSL2 as rung zero — what it proves, and the exact wall it hits
siblings.summary: WSL2 retires every userland risk in a Linux migration and none of the machine-ownership risks; here is where the line falls in 2026.

siblings.title: Dual-boot Linux next to Windows in 2026 without wrecking the Windows install
siblings.summary: Buy a second NVMe, keep the two OSes ignorant of each other, and pick Linux from the firmware boot menu — the layout with the smallest blast radius on your Windows install.

siblings.title: Trial hardware and VM paths for evaluating Linux before you commit (2026)
siblings.summary: Live USB first (€10, 15 minutes, proves your actual hardware), then a full install on an external NVMe SSD (€90–150) — everything else is a detour.

siblings.title: Living in both OSes: running Windows and Linux for months without your setup rotting
siblings.summary: One source of truth per asset class, replicated by a tool that knows the OS difference — never a shared partition and never two hand-edited copies.

siblings.title: Exit criteria and the blocker inventory: decide the Linux switch on evidence, not vibes
siblings.summary: A fill-in blocker inventory plus tickable go/no-go criteria and a pre-committed rollback date for a Windows-to-Linux workstation trial.

sources.title: Dropbox system requirements
sources.claim: Official 2026 Linux requirements: Dropbox folder must sit on ext4, zfs, eCryptFS (backed by ext4), xfs or btrfs; LAN sync is IPv4-only; ARM unsupported.

sources.title: Dropbox Community — sharing one folder between Windows and Linux installs
sources.claim: One on-disk Dropbox folder cannot be shared between Windows and Linux installs because the clients have no supported filesystem in common.

sources.title: git-remote-dropbox
sources.claim: The Dropbox desktop client can corrupt git repositories; git-remote-dropbox uses the API directly instead of the desktop client.

sources.title: maestral (GitHub)
sources.claim: Maestral, the leading open-source Dropbox client for Linux/macOS, was archived on 2026-07-28.

sources.title: It's FOSS — Dropbox to support ext4 only on Linux
sources.claim: Dropbox announced in August 2018 that from 7 November 2018 only ext4 would be supported on Linux.

sources.title: The Register — Dropbox drops encrypted Linux filesystems
sources.claim: The filesystem restriction exists because Dropbox stores file identity in extended attributes.

sources.title: It's FOSS — Dropbox brings back Linux filesystem support
sources.claim: Dropbox restored zfs and xfs (64-bit) plus btrfs and eCryptFS in beta build 77.3.127, July 2019.

sources.title: dropbox-filesystem-fix
sources.claim: dropbox-filesystem-fix is an LD_PRELOAD shim patching the client's filesystem detection; archived November 2025, tested only to client 89.4.278.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — delete files
sources.claim: Deleting a file inside a shared folder removes it for every member, not just locally.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — recover deleted files and folders
sources.claim: Dropbox keeps deleted files and prior versions for 30-365 days depending on plan, and Rewind can undo mass deletions.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — Smart Sync / online-only files
sources.claim: Smart Sync / online-only files are documented for Windows and Mac only, not Linux.

sources.title: Dropbox Forum — when will online-only files work on Linux
sources.claim: Online-only files on Linux is a long-standing user request with no Dropbox commitment.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — selective sync overview
sources.claim: Selective sync is per-device and folder-granular; individual files cannot be selected.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — ignored files
sources.claim: Linux ignore uses the com.dropbox.ignored xattr per file/folder, is not pattern-based, needs the default Dropbox folder location, and removes the content from the server and other devices.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — Linux commands
sources.claim: The Linux CLI ships help, start, autostart, proxy, lansync, throttle, running, status, filestatus, ls, sharelink, stop and exclude.

sources.title: nautilus-dropbox
sources.claim: File-manager integration on Linux is provided only by the official nautilus-dropbox extension, which builds against GTK4 Nautilus.

sources.title: TechRepublic — run Dropbox from a headless Linux server
sources.claim: Headless Linux use runs the tarball's ~/.dropbox-dist/dropboxd and links the account via a pasted URL, controlled by dropbox.py.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — desktop app for Linux
sources.claim: The Linux desktop app requires GTK 2.24, GDK 2.24, Glib 2.40 and LibAppIndicator 12.10; only Ubuntu 18.04+ and Fedora 28+ are supported; LXDE cannot be supported. Page updated 9 Feb 2026.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — do shared folders count against storage
sources.claim: A shared folder counts against every member's quota unless all members share a Standard/Advanced/Enterprise team or Family plan.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — conflicted copy
sources.claim: Conflicted copies arise from simultaneous edits, offline edits, or a file left open in an auto-saving app on another machine.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — computer limit
sources.claim: Dropbox Basic allows only three linked devices at a time; a dual-boot machine consumes two slots.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — symlinks
sources.claim: Symlinks pointing outside the Dropbox folder sync as link files only; Windows Dropbox does not support symlinks or junctions at all.

sources.title: shkspr.mobi — case conflicts in Dropbox for Linux
sources.claim: Case-only-differing names created on Linux get mangled by Dropbox because the namespace behaves case-insensitively across platforms.

sources.title: rclone — Dropbox backend
sources.claim: rclone's Dropbox backend documents case-insensitivity, restricted filenames, mtime-only-on-reupload, a 10000-file purge limit, and --dropbox-shared-folders for shared folders.

sources.title: Maestral docs — inotify limits
sources.claim: Sync daemons consume one inotify watch per directory; the historic default is 8192, Dropbox recommends 100000, and kernels 5.11+ auto-scale to 1048576.

sources.title: Maestral
sources.claim: Maestral is unmaintained as of June 2026 and will only work until its certificates expire; it offers selective sync, .mignore gitignore patterns and no device cap.

sources.title: Maestral — about
sources.claim: Maestral syncs shared folders but cannot manage Dropbox Paper, teams, or shared-folder settings.

sources.title: rclone — bisync
sources.claim: rclone bisync is explicitly flagged as advanced with data-loss risk if the limitations are not understood.

sources.title: Syncthing
sources.claim: Syncthing is peer-to-peer with no central server, so it cannot participate in a Dropbox shared folder.

sources.title: dbxfs
sources.claim: dbxfs mounts a Dropbox account as a FUSE filesystem, the only Linux route to online-only access; current version 2.0.1, Python 3.11+, GPLv3.

sources.title: dbxfs (GitHub mirror)
sources.claim: The dbxfs GitHub repository was archived in July 2021 and development moved off GitHub.

sources.title: Insync — pricing
sources.claim: Insync Desktop is a one-time $39.99 per cloud account with unlimited machines; the Server plan is $159.99/year per machine.

sources.title: Insync for Linux
sources.claim: Insync is a commercial Linux client supporting Google Drive, OneDrive and Dropbox including Dropbox team folders.

sources.title: Dropbox Help — file names
sources.claim: Dropbox rejects the characters \ / : * ? " < > | and names beyond roughly 255 characters including path.
